'''Raymond F. Schinazi''' (born 21 March 1950) is an Egyptian-born organic [[medicinal chemist]]. He is the Frances Winship Walters Professor of Pediatrics at [[Emory University]]. He has expertise in antiviral agents, pharmacology, and biotechnology. His research focuses on developing treatments for infections caused by [[human immunodeficiency virus]] (HIV), [[hepatitis B]] (HBV), [[hepatitis C]] (HCV), [[herpes]], [[dengue fever]], [[yellow fever]], [[Mpox]], [[norovirus]], [[zika]], [[chikungunya]], and other emerging viruses. These treatment options include antiviral agents as well as synthetic, biochemical, pharmacological and molecular genetic approaches, including molecular modeling and [[gene therapy]].<ref name="Yerkes">{{cite web |title=Yerkes -- Raymond Schinazi,PhD|url=http://www.yerkes.emory.edu/research/divisions/emory_vaccine_center/schinazi_raymond.html |website=Emory |access-date=6 July 2020}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
[[File:Raymond Schinazi with Dr William H Prusoff.jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|right|Schinazi with Yale mentor Dr William H Prusoff]]
Schinazi was born on March 21, 1950, in [[Alexandria]], Egypt to [[History of the Jews in Egypt|Italian-Jewish parents]].<ref name="Ahram">{{cite web |title=Egyptian-born hep C drug inventor meets health minister|url=http://english.ahram.org.eg/NewsContent/1/64/111764/Egypt/Politics-/AboutUs.aspx |website=Ahram Online |access-date=6 July 2020 |language=en |date=26 Sep 2014}}</ref> In 1962, his family was sequestered by the [[Gamal Abdel Nasser|Nasser]] regime and in 1964 they immigrated to [[Naples]], Italy as refugees. Schinazi went to boarding school at Carmel College, England, where he completed his early education before being admitted as an undergraduate at the [[University of Bath]] in 1968. He received his BSc in chemistry in 1972, and remained at Bath to complete his PhD in 1976. In 2006 he was awarded an honorary doctorate in Biotechnology from the University of Bath. In 1976, he moved to [[Yale University]]'s department of pharmacology and trained as a postdoctoral fellow with [[William Prusoff]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Cookson |first=Clive |date=July 27, 2014 |title=Raymond Schinazi fled Nasser's Egypt to become pioneer in antivirals |website=[[Financial Times]] |url=https://www.ft.com/content/e7925e46-fc86-11e3-86dc-00144feab7de |url-access=subscription |access-date=June 8, 2018}}</ref><ref name="joncohen.org">{{cite web|url=http://joncohen.org/2015/05/08/king-of-the-pills/|title=King of the pills|date=8 May 2015|website=Joncohen.org|access-date=8 June 2018}}</ref><ref name="pedsresearch.org">{{cite web|url=http://www.pedsresearch.org/people/faculty/raymond-schinazi-phd|title=Atlanta Pediatric Research - Raymond Schinazi, PhD, DSc - Faculty - People - Emory + Children's + GT - Atlanta Pediatric Research Alliance|website=Pedsresearch.org|access-date=8 June 2018}}</ref>

He also completed postdoctoral trainings in virology at the [[University of Chicago]] with [[Bernard Roizman]] and at [[University of North Carolina]] with [[Cheng_Yung-chi|Yung-Chi Cheng]], and virology/immunology at Emory University with André Nahmias.

== Career ==
Schinazi is currently the Frances Winship Walters Professor of Pediatrics, Director of the Laboratory of Biochemical Pharmacology<ref name="pedsresearch.org"/> at Emory University, where he has served since 1978.<ref name="scrip.pharmamedtechbi.com">{{cite web|url=https://scrip.pharmamedtechbi.com/SC098185/Where-Theres-A-Cure-Theres-Controversy-Raymond-Schinazis-Story|title=Where There's A Cure There's Controversy: Raymond Schinazi's Story|date=February 13, 2017|website=Scrip.pharmamedtechbi.com|access-date=June 8, 2018}}</ref> He also holds Adjunct Professor positions at both [[University of Georgia]] (Atlanta, GA)<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.uga-cdd.org/facultydetail.php?id=29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080102010914/http://www.uga-cdd.org/facultydetail.php?id=29|archive-date=January 2, 2008|title=UGA Center for Drug Discovery Faculty|first=Plexus Web|last=Creations|website=Uga-cdd.org|access-date=June 8, 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref> and [[University of Miami]] (Miami, Florida).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://medicine.med.miami.edu/infectious-diseases/faculty-list|title=Division of Infectious Diseases at Miller School of Medicine|website=medicine.med.miami.edu|access-date=June 8, 2018}}</ref> He worked part-time for the Emory University affiliated Atlanta VA for 35 years while maintaining his Emory University appointment, retiring from the VA in 2016.<ref name="atlantajewishtimes.timesofisrael.com">{{cite web|url=http://atlantajewishtimes.timesofisrael.com/emory-virologist-raymond-schinazi-honored/|title=Emory Virologist Raymond Schinazi Honored|website=Atlanta Jewish Times|date=December 6, 2016}}</ref>

He began his work as a herpes virologist with a specific focus on developing drug therapeutics for orolabial and genital herpes and severe life-threatening infections like herpes encephalitis. When HIV was identified as a virus in the 1980s, Schinazi and his fellow researchers directed their attention towards the problem. He was able to translate his knowledge gained through his work on the herpes viruses towards addressing HIV and HBV. He is credited for setting up the first-ever HIV laboratory at Emory University complete with a protocol on how to handle the dangerous virus in the laboratory setting so he and his team could pursue the development of novel antiviral drugs.<ref name="pedsresearch.org"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://news.emory.edu/stories/2014/11/schinazi_liver_foundation_award/index.html|title=American Liver Foundation awards Emory inventor with Distinguished Scientific Achievement Award|date=November 21, 2014|website=news.emory.edu}}</ref> In 1987, he helped Prusoff's laboratory discover that d4T, a nucleoside analog, had selective activity against HIV.<ref name="joncohen.org"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/03/19/opinion/the-scientists-story.html|title=The Scientist's Story|first=William|last=Prusoff|date=March 19, 2001|access-date=June 8, 2018|website=[[New York Times]]}}</ref>

[[File:Raymond Schinazi with the famous Berlin Patient.jpg|thumb|upright|Schinazi with the famous Berlin Patient - the first person presumed cured of HIV]]

[[File:Raymond Schinazi with Magic Johnson.jpg|thumb|upright|Raymond Schinazi with US basketball legend Magic Johnson, who has been living with HIV - with the aid of drugs Schinazi helped to discover and develop - since 1991]]

Schinazi is best known for his involvement in the discovery and development of innovative anti-HIV, HBV, and HCV drugs on the market. To date, he has been involved in the development of five FDA-approved drugs of which three are used in eight different drug combinations.<ref name="joncohen.org"/> More than 94% of HIV-positive people take at least one of the drugs he invented.<ref name="atlantajewishtimes.timesofisrael.com"/><ref name="scrip.pharmamedtechbi.com"/> He has authored more than 550 peer-reviewed papers in academic literature with over 20,000 total citations.<ref name="Publons">{{cite web |title=Raymond F Schinazi's Publons profile |url=https://publons.com/researcher/2158884/raymond-f-schinazi/ |website=Publons.com |access-date=6 July 2020 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.scopus.com/|title=Scopus preview|website=Scopus.com|access-date=June 8, 2018}}</ref>

==Discovery and development of [[lamivudine]] (3TC)==
Among the first drugs discovered and developed for treatment of HIV came through the collaboration between [[Dennis C. Liotta]] (Emory) and Schinazi. In 1992, they first published on lamivudine (3TC) in [[Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1128/AAC.36.3.672 |pmid=1320365 |pmc=190578 |title=Activities of the four optical isomers of 2',3'-dideoxy-3'-thiacytidine (BCH-189) against human immunodeficiency virus type 1 in human lymphocytes |journal=Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy |volume=36 |issue=3 |pages=672–6 |year=1992 |last1=Schinazi |first1=R F |last2=Chu |first2=C K |last3=Peck |first3=A |last4=McMillan |first4=A |last5=Mathis |first5=R |last6=Cannon |first6=D |last7=Jeong |first7=L S |last8=Beach |first8=J W |last9=Choi |first9=W B |last10=Yeola |first10=S }}</ref> This drug became one of the most successful antiviral agents used to combat HIV as part of fixed-dose combinations (including Combivir, Trizivir, Epzicom, and Triumeq). Combination therapies incorporating 3TC quickly became the standard of care, with safe and effective nucleoside [[reverse transcriptase]] (RF) inhibitors, such as 3TC and its related cousins, serving as the cornerstones of combination chemotherapy.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/gathering-hivaids-pioneers-raw-memories-mix-current-conflicts|title=At gathering of HIV/AIDS pioneers, raw memories mix with current conflicts|date=25 October 2016|website=Sciencemag.org|access-date=8 June 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |pmid=18472979 |pmc=2374941 |year=2007 |last1=Portsmouth |first1=S. D |title=The renaissance of fixed dose combinations: Combivir |journal=Therapeutics and Clinical Risk Management |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=579–83 |last2=Scott |first2=C. J }}</ref> 3TC was also found to be active against HBV in collaboration with Drs. Dennis Liotta, Philip Furman and Yung-Chi Cheng.<ref name=US7468436B2>{{cite patent| country = U.S.| number = US7468436B2| status = Expired - Fee Related| title  = Method of resolution and antiviral activity of 1,3-oxathiolane nucleoside enantiomers| pubdate = 2004-09-02| gdate  = 008-12-23| fdate  = 2004-03-05| pridate = 1990-02-01| invent1 = Dennis C. Liotta| invent2 = Raymond F. Schinazi| invent3 = Woo-Baeg Choi| assign1 = Emory University| assign2 = | class  = | url  = https://patents.google.com/patent/US7468436B2/en}}</ref><ref>{{cite patent
| country = U.S.| number = US7160999B2| status = Expired | title  = Method of resolution and antiviral activity of 1,3-oxathiolane nucleoside enantiomers| pubdate = 2004-02-26| gdate  = | fdate  = 2003-08-20| pridate = 1990-02-01
| invent1 = Dennis C. Liotta| invent2 = Raymond F. Schinazi| invent3 = Woo-Baeg Choi| assign1 = Emory University| assign2 =
| class  = | url  = https://patents.google.com/patent/US7160999B2/en}}</ref><ref name="medicinespatentpool.org">{{cite web |url=http://www.medicinespatentpool.org/wp-content/uploads/54-57.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=February 14, 2018 |archive-date=October 3, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211003045137/https://medicinespatentpool.org/wp-content/uploads/54-57.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Discovery and development of emtricitabine [(-)-FTC or FTC] ==
Schinazi's work led to the discovery of a second nucleoside analog, [[emtricitabine]] (FTC), subsequently resulting in a potent, safe nucleoside analog commonly used in treatment regimens.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.emory.edu/news/Releases/emtri/|title=Emory University signs $525 million agreement with Gilead, Royalty Pharma|website=Emory.edu|access-date=June 8, 2018}}</ref> The discovery of FTC was first published in 1992 in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy as another new anti-HIV compound.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1128/AAC.36.11.2423 |pmid=1283296 |pmc=284347 |title=Selective inhibition of human immunodeficiency viruses by racemates and enantiomers of cis-5-fluoro-1-&#91;2-(hydroxymethyl)-1,3-oxathiolan-5-yl&#93;cytosine |journal=Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy |volume=36 |issue=11 |pages=2423–31 |year=1992 |last1=Schinazi |first1=R F |last2=McMillan |first2=A |last3=Cannon |first3=D |last4=Mathis |first4=R |last5=Lloyd |first5=R M |last6=Peck |first6=A |last7=Sommadossi |first7=J P |last8=St Clair |first8=M |last9=Wilson |first9=J |last10=Furman |first10=P A }}</ref> The mechanism of action of FTC is by incorporation of FTC-TP into the growing viral DNA strand results in chain termination, disrupting viral DNA synthesis. Disruption of this process results in rapid reduction of systemic viral loads to undetectable in HIV-infected individuals, effectively allowing for significant rebound of CD4+ T-cells, effectively providing a tandem mechanism resulting in control of systemic viremia and restoration of functional immunity. 

To secure the commercial rights to the compound, Gilead Sciences acquired Triangle Pharmaceuticals in 2003 for $464 million, subsequently marketing the drug under the brand name Emtriva.<ref name="WSJ_Triangle">{{cite news |title=Gilead to Pay 464 Million For Triangle Pharmaceuticals |url=https://wsj.com |work=The Wall Street Journal |date=December 4, 2002}}</ref><ref name="CEN_Emory">{{cite news |last1=Ainsworth |first1=Susan J. |title=Emory Gets 525 Million for AIDS Drug |url=https://acs.org |work=Chemical & Engineering News |date=July 25, 2005}}</ref> Triangle had originally licensed the molecule from Emory University in 1996, and was itself co-founded by Schinazi and Liotta in 1995 as a vehicle to develop their academic discoveries.<ref name="BizJournals_Triangle">{{cite news |title=From credit card to $40M |url=https://bizjournals.com |work=Atlanta Business Chronicle |date=August 23, 2004}}</ref> In July 2005, Gilead teamed with Royalty Pharma to completely buy out Emory University's remaining royalty interests in emtricitabine for a one-time cash payment of $525 million.<ref name="Gilead_Emory_PR">{{cite web |title=Gilead Sciences and Royalty Pharma Announce 525 Million Agreement with Emory University to Purchase Royalty Interest for Emtricitabine |url=https://gilead.com |publisher=Gilead Sciences |date=July 18, 2005}}</ref> At the time of execution, the transaction stood as the largest intellectual property rights payoff in the history of American higher education, establishing an unprecedented valuation baseline for academic technology transfer to the pharmaceutical industry.<ref name="InsideHigherEd_Emory">{{cite news |title=2 Companies Will Pay Emory 525 Million for Drug Royalties |url=https://insidehighered.com |work=Inside Higher Ed |date=July 19, 2005}}</ref>

In addition, FTC in combination with [[Emtricitabine/tenofovir|tenofovir disoproxil fumarate]] (Truvada) was approved as a prophylactic drug (part of PrEP) to prevent transmission of HIV, further broadening its use beyond HIV-positive people to that of prophylaxis, underscoring a novel and previously unmet need with ramifications for global health worldwide. Today, this drug is widely used as part of fixed-dose combination drug regimens, including Truvada, Atripla, Complera, Stribild, Descovy, Genvoya, Odefsey, Descovy, Biktarvy, and Symtuza.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aidsmap.com/resources/treatmentsdirectory/drugs/FTC-emtricitabine-iEmtrivai/page/1731063/|title=A to Z of antiretroviral drugs - Emtricitabine (Emtriva)|website=Aidsmap.com|access-date=June 8, 2018}}</ref><ref name="medicinespatentpool.org"/> Like 3TC, FTC was found to be active against HBV, but was never approved for this indication by the US FDA.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US5914331A/en|title=Antiviral activity and resolution of 2-hydroxymethyl-5-(5-fluorocytosin-1-yl)-1,3-oxathiolane|website=Patents.google.com|access-date=June 8, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite patent| country= United States
| number= US7115584B2| status= Expired - Fee Related| title= HIV-1 mutations selected for by β-2′,3′-didehydro-2′,3′-dideoxy-5-fluorocytidine| pubdate= October 3, 2006| gdate= October 3, 2006| fdate= 2003-01-23| pridate= 1999-01-22| inventor= Raymond F. Schinazi| invent1= Jennifer L. Hammond| invent2= John W. Mellors| invent3       = Dennis C. Liotta| assign1= | assign2= | class= | url= https://patents.google.com/patent/US7115584B2/en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US6642245B1/en|title=Antiviral activity and resolution of 2-hydroxymethyl-5-(5-fluorocytosin-1-yl)-1,3-oxathiolane|website=Patents.google.com|access-date=June 8, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US6232300B1/en|title=Treatment of HIV by administration of β-D-2′, 3′-didehydro-2′,3′-dideoxy-5-fluorocytidine (D4FC)|website=Patents.google.com|access-date=June 8, 2018}}</ref>

== Sofosbuvir (Sovaldi) ==
In 2004, Schinazi was the principal founder of [[Pharmasset]], a company that would later go on to develop [[sofosbuvir]].<ref name="Sachs">{{cite web |last1=Sachs |first1=Jeffrey |title=The Drug That Is Bankrupting America |url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/the-drug-that-is-bankrupt_b_6692340 |website=HuffPost |access-date=6 July 2020 |language=en |date=Apr 18, 2015}}</ref> The name Pharmasset was derived from 'pharmaceutical assets' and the original business plan was to create assets that would be sold to other companies.<ref name="Berkrot">{{cite web |last1=Berkrot |first1=Bill |title=Gilead could have had Pharmasset cheap: founder |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-pharmasset-founder/gilead-could-have-had-pharmasset-cheap-founder-idUSTRE7AL2ES20111122 |website=Reuters |access-date=6 July 2020 |date=22 November 2011}}</ref> The company raised around $45M in its 2007 IPO at $9 per share. It would later be taken over at $137 per share. In November 2011, [[Gilead Sciences]] announced a takeover bid for Pharmasset for approximately $11.4 billion.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://investors.gilead.com/phoenix.zhtml?ID=1632335&c=69964&p=irol-newsArticle|title=Gilead Sciences to Acquire Pharmasset, Inc. for $11 Billion|website=investors.gilead.com|access-date=8 June 2018|archive-date=15 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171115204331/http://investors.gilead.com/phoenix.zhtml?c=69964&p=irol-newsArticle&ID=1632335|url-status=dead}}</ref>Gilead commercialized the compound under the trade name Sovaldi, which later served as the active therapeutic backbone for the pan-genotypic fixed-dose combination therapies Harvoni (sofosbuvir/ledipasvir) and Epclusa (sofosbuvir/velpatasvir).<ref name="EMA_Harvoni">{{cite web |title=Harvoni: EPAR |url=https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/EPAR/harvoni |publisher=European Medicines Agency |access-date=2026-10-27}}</ref><ref name="FDA_Epclusa">{{cite web |title=Epclusa Prescribing Information |url=https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2016/208341s000lbl.pdf |publisher=U.S. Food and Drug Administration |access-date=2026-10-27}}</ref>

Schinazi's contribution to the discovery of sofosbuvir is contentious. He is the co-author of a 2005 paper that discovered a precursor to the drug.<ref name=pmid25953989>{{cite journal |doi=10.1126/science.348.6235.622 |pmid=25953989 |title=King of the pills |journal=Science |volume=348 |issue=6235 |pages=622–5 |year=2015 |last1=Cohen |first1=J |bibcode=2015Sci...348..622C |doi-access=free }}</ref> Jean-Pierre Sommadossi, who co-founded both Pharmasset and Idenix with Schinazi, served as the principal founder of Idenix. <ref name="Roy2020">{{cite journal |last1=Roy |first1=Vikas |title=Public funding for transformative drugs: the case of sofosbuvir |journal=Journal of Law and the Biosciences |date=1 October 2020 |volume=7 |issue=1 |doi=10.1093/jlb/lsaa066 |pmid=33014451}}</ref>In litigation between Idenix and Gilead/Pharmasset, there was an Order denying Idenix's motion for enhanced damages where the court noted that Schinazi "violated his confidentially obligations to Idenix, and shared with Pharmasset scientists Idenix's proprietary discoveries relating to treatment of HCV".{{Sfn|C.A. No. 14-846-LPS|2017|p=7}} However, even “fully accepting Idenix’s view of the evidence,” it was the company Schinazi founded, Pharmasset, not Idenix, that synthesized the key “compound that led to a cure for HCV.”.{{Sfn|C.A. No. 14-846-LPS|2017|p=15}} Even accepting that Idenix discovered a component of the compound, the cure for HCV was discovered only after Pharmasset/Gilead's ”revolutionary refinement of that invention.”{{Sfn|C.A. No. 14-846-LPS|2017|pp=15-16}} Patent law, according to the order, reflects a balance between protection “and the importance of facilitating the imitation and refinement through imitation that are necessary to invention itself and the very lifeblood of a competitive economy.”{{Sfn|C.A. No. 14-846-LPS|2017|pp=7, 16}}

[[File:Schinazi in Egypt.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|right|Schinazi returning to Egypt - for the first time in 50 years since his family fled the Nasser regime as refugees in 1964]]

In 2014, Schinazi, working with the Egyptian government and Gilead Sciences, agreed to provide Egypt with the drug Sofosbuvir (Sovaldi) for about US$1,000, which is only one percent of its market price. Also working with Pharco, an Egyptian Pharmaceutical company Sovaldi is now available for less than US$120 per cure.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Pew5yUmo-W0.|title=
CNN Marketplace Africa - Dr. Sherine Helmy speaks about Hepatitis C Eradication|website=youtube.com|access-date=26 June 2026}}</ref>
 
Prior to the implementation of a nationwide screening and treatment program for hepatitis C in 2014, there were over 6 million Egyptians infected and living with the disease.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6129a2.htm|title=Progress Toward Prevention and Control of Hepatitis C Virus Infection — Egypt, 2001–2012|website=cdc.gov|access-date=26 June 2026}}</ref>
But between 2014 and 2018, over 60 million people were screened and more than 4.1 million treated.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.emro.who.int/media/news/egypt-becomes-the-first-country-to-achieve-who-validation-on-the-path-to-elimination-of-hepatitis-c.html|title=Egypt becomes the first country to achieve WHO validation on the path to elimination of hepatitis C|website=emro.who.int|access-date=26 June 2026}}</ref>  <ref>{{Cite web|url=https://english.ahram.org.eg/UI/Front/Inner.aspx?NewsContentID=467432|title=Egypt’s success treating hepatitis C a ‘lighthouse’ for rest of world, says Raymond Schinazi|website=english.ahram.org.eg|access-date=26 June 2026}}</ref>

== Other drugs ==
Schinazi has also had a hand in the development of the other FDA-approved drugs [[stavudine]] and [[telbivudine]].<ref name=pmid25953989/>

== Honors and awards ==
[[File:Schinazi Holy Award.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|Schinazi receiving the 2025 Antonín Holý Award]]

In 2018, Schinazi received the [[Legion of Honour|Chevalier de la Légion d’honneur]], the French Legion of Honor, with the rank of knight.<ref name="french legion">{{cite web |last1=Korschun |first1=Holly |title=Emory HIV/AIDS drug inventor, entrepreneur decorated with French Legion of Honor |url=http://news.emory.edu/stories/2018/12/schinazi_award/ |website=Emory |access-date=6 July 2020 |language=en |date=4 December 2018}}</ref> Established in 1802 by Napoleon Bonaparte, it is the highest decoration bestowed in France and recognizes outstanding service to the French Republic. 

In the years before and since, he has the recipient of numerous other awards, including: the Bruce Witte (Blumberg) Annual Distinguished Award- Hepatitis B Foundation (2000);<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.biomedinvestors.com/raymond-schinazi/ |title=Bio/Med Investor Network |access-date=9 January 2019 |archive-date=9 January 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190109062405/http://www.biomedinvestors.com/raymond-schinazi/) |url-status=dead }}</ref> the Georgia Biomedical Industry Growth Award (2003),<ref name="GA BIG Award">{{cite web |title=THE VALUE OF INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY|url=https://www.gc.cuny.edu/news/press-release-value-intellectual-property |website=gc.cuny.edu |access-date=26 June 2026}}</ref> Distinguished Scientist Award- Hepatitis B Foundation (2006);<ref name="Farley">{{cite press release|last1=Farley |first1=Peggy |title=Hepatitis B Foundation Presents Distinguished Scientist Award 2006 to Emory University Professor Dr. Raymond F. Schinazi, a Pioneer in Antiviral Drug Discovery Research for HIV and Hepatitis B |url=http://www.releasewire.com/press-releases/release-5726.htm |access-date=6 July 2020 |work=ReleaseWire |agency=SBWIRE |date=22 March 2006 |location=Doylestown, PA}}</ref> Emory University's Dean's Distinguished Faculty Lecture and Award (2008);<ref name="Lawley">{{cite web |last1=Lawley |first1=Thomas J. MD |title=Emory School of Medicine - Dean's Letter |url=http://whsc.emory.edu/_pubs/deans_letters_som/2008/april/ |website=Emory |access-date=6 July 2020 |date=April 2008 |archive-date=16 November 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211116171636/http://whsc.emory.edu/_pubs/deans_letters_som/2008/april/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Inductee- Technology Hall of Fame of Georgia (2011);<ref>{{cite web | author1=Pricewaterhousecoopers | url=http://www.pwc.com/us/en/press-releases/2016/technology-hall-of-fame-of-georgia-press-release.html | title=US Newsroom |website=Pwc.com}}</ref> Intellectual Property Legends Award - Georgia State University (2012);<ref name="Emory-IPL Award"> {{cite web |title=Honors for Wagner, Young, Liotta and Schinazi, Nemenman and García |url=https://news.emory.edu/stories/2012/10/honors-wagner-young-liotta-and-schinazi-nemenman-and-garcia/ |website=news.emory.edu |access-date=30 June 2026}}</ref> Charter Fellow- National Academy of Inventors (2013);<ref>{{cite web | url=http://news.emory.edu/stories/2012/12/nai_charter_fellows_wagner_schinazi/campus.html | title=Wagner, Schinazi named National Academy of Inventors Charter Fellows - Emory University; Atlanta GA|website=News.emory.edu}}</ref> Distinguished Medical Science Award- Friends of the National Library of Medicine (2013);<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.fnlm.org/events_2013.php |title=Friends of the National Library of Medicine |access-date=9 January 2019 |archive-date=20 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180620083031/http://www.fnlm.org/events_2013.php |url-status=dead }}</ref> Distinguished Scientific Achievement Award- American Liver Foundation (2014);<ref>{{cite web | url=http://news.emory.edu/stories/2014/11/schinazi_liver_foundation_award/index.html | title=American Liver Foundation awards Emory inventor with Distinguished Scientific Achievement Award - Emory University - Atlanta GA |website=News.emory.edu}}</ref> Research & Hope Award for Excellence in Academic Research- PhRMA Foundation (2014);<ref>{{cite web |title=PhRMA organization honors Emory scientist with Excellence in Academic Research award |url=https://news.emory.edu/stories/2014/08/phrma-organization-honors-emory-scientist-excellence-academic-research-award/ |website=news.emory.edu |date=August 27, 2014 |access-date=30 June 2026}}</ref> William S. Middleton Award- US Veterans Affairs (2015);<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.research.va.gov/currents/0815-10.cfm | title=Raymond Schinazi, drug-development pioneer, earns VA's highest honor for biomedical research |website=Research.va.gov}}</ref> Tom Glaser Leadership Award- Connexx Eagle Star Awards (2015);<ref name="Glaser">{{cite web |title=Emory Virologist Raymond Schinazi Honored |url=https://www.atlantajewishtimes.com/emory-virologist-raymond-schinazi-honored |website=atlantajewishtimes.com|date=6 December 2016 |access-date=26 June 2026}}</ref> Lifetime Achievement Award- Scrip Award, London (2016);<ref name="scrip">{{cite web |author1=Scrip Team |title=Industry's Achievements Lauded At 12th Annual Scrip Awards |url=https://scrip.pharmaintelligence.informa.com/SC097768/Industrys-Achievements-Lauded-At-12supthsup-Annual-Scrip-Awards |website=Scrip Pharma Intelligence |access-date=6 July 2020 |date=30 November 2016}}</ref> Lifetime Achievement Award for Public Service- Institute of Human Virology (2016);<ref name="Korschun">{{cite web |last1=Korschun |first1=Holly |title=Institute of Human Virology honors Schinazi with Lifetime Achievement Awards |url=http://news.emory.edu/stories/2016/09/schinazi_ihv_awards/ |website=Emory |access-date=6 July 2020 |date=22 September 2016}}</ref>; Global Hepatitis Award from the International Symposium on [[Viral hepatitis|Viral Hepatitis]] and Liver Disease (ISVHLD) 2018;<ref name="french legion"/> Distinguished Achievement Award- American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)(2021).<ref>{{cite web |title=AASLD Distinguished Achievement Award for Raymond F Schinazi|url=https://www.aasld.org/news/aasld-distinguished-achievement-award-raymond-f-schinazi-pdf-faasld |publisher=American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases| access-date=30 June 2026}}</ref>

Schinazi became a Fellow of the American Association 
for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) in 2020,<ref>{{cite web |title=AAAS Announces Leading Scientists Elected as 2020 Fellows|url=https://www.aaas.org/news/aaas-announces-leading-scientists-elected-2020-fellows 
|publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science | access-date=30 June 2026}}</ref> and received an Honorary Doctorate (''Doctor Philosophiae Honoris Causa'') from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in 2023. <ref name="Hebrew">{{cite web |title=Hebrew University Confers Honorary Doctorate Degree on Dr. Raymond Schinazi, Renowned HIV Researcher and Emory University Professor |url=https://www.afhu.org/2023/06/15/hebrew-university-confers-honorary-doctorate-degree-on-dr-raymond-schinazi-renowned-hiv-researcher-and-emory-university-professor/ |website=ahfu.org |date=15 June 2023 |access-date=26 June 2026}}</ref> In the same year, Schinazi and colleagues received the "Deal of the Year" award from Emory's Office of Technology Transfer for their licensing agreement with Pfizer, Inc.<ref name="Pfizer">{{cite web |title=Annual Celebration of Technology and Innovation 2023|url=https://ott.emory.edu/resources/annual23/index.html |website=Emory |access-date=26 June 2026}}</ref>

[[File:Schinazi Receiving An Honorary Degree at Uppsala University.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|Schinazi receiving his honorary doctorate at [[Uppsala University]], 2025]]

In 2025, he received the Antonín Holý Memorial Award from the [[International Society for Antiviral Research]] (ISAR) in recognition of his career-long prominence and achievements in antiviral drug discovery and development<ref name="Antonin Holy Award">{{cite web |title=Antonín Holý Memorial Award |url=https://www.isar-icar.com/Awards/ |website=isar-icar.com |access-date=12 July 2026}}</ref>. In the same year, he was also inducted into the Georgia Technology Hall of Fame <ref name="GA HoF">{{cite web|title=Georgia Technology Hall of Fame|url=https://www.tagonline.org/award/georgia-technology-hall-of-fame/ |website=tagonline.org |access-date=26 June 2026}}</ref> and received an Honorary Doctorate in Medicine from Uppsala University. <ref name="Uppsala">{{cite web |title=New honorary doctors at the University |url=https://www.uu.se/en/staff/news/2025/2025-01-14-new-honorary-doctors-at-the-university |website= Uppsala Universitet |date=January 14, 2025 |access-date=26 June 2026}}</ref>. 

In 2026, he received the Emory University President's Medal alongside his colleagues [[Dennis Liotta]] and Woo-Baeg Choi, in recognition of their transformative contributions to global public health via life-saving HIV medications - estimated to be taken by over 90% of people living with HIV in the United States and by millions more worldwide.
<ref name="Emory-Presidents-medal">{{cite web |title=President’s Medal honors biomedical researchers who developed lifesaving HIV medications|url=https://news.emory.edu/stories/2026/05/presidents-medal-honors-biomedical-researchers-who-developed-lifesaving-hiv|access-date=30 June 2026}}</ref>

== Podcast, radio, and online interviews ==
Schinazi has discussed his life, career and research in numerous podcast, radio, and video interviews, including the BBC Radio 4 programme ''The Life Scientific''<ref>{{cite episode |title=Raymond Schinazi on revolutionising treatments for HIV and Hepatitis C |series=The Life Scientific |credits=Al-Khalili, Jim |network=BBC Radio 4 |date=16 July 2024 |url=https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/raymond-schinazi-on-revolutionising-treatments-for/id469912037?i=1000662382560}}</ref>, ''The Road From Carmel''<ref name=Carmel>{{cite episode |title=Ray Schinazi (1964-68)|series=The Road From Carmel |date=12 December 2023|url=https://sites.libsyn.com/489671/ray-schinazi-1964-68}}</ref>, and the IAS-USA series ''Going Anti-Viral''.<ref>{{cite episode |title=Development of a Hepatitis C Cure with Dr Raymond Schinazi |series=Going Anti-Viral |credits=Saag, Michael |number=46 |publisher=IAS-USA |date=April 2025 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TLcYF-X-zwo}}</ref> He has also been featured in a two-part interview series for the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine's ''Inside U Miami Medicine'' podcast<ref>{{cite episode |title=Drug Pioneer and Trailblazer: The Dr. Raymond Schinazi Story (Part 1) |series=Inside U Miami Medicine |publisher=University of Miami Miller School of Medicine |date=March 2024 |url=https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/drug-pioneer-and-trailblazer-the-dr-raymond/id1653458353?i=1000650759303}}</ref><ref>{{cite episode |title=Curing Hepatitis C: The Dr. Raymond Schinazi Story (Part 2) |series=Inside U Miami Medicine |publisher=University of Miami Miller School of Medicine |date=April 2024 |url=https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/curing-hepatitis-c-the-dr-raymond-schinazi-story-part-2/id1653458353?i=1000652241634}}</ref> and a video interview with Dr. Michael Lederman and Dr. Neil Greenspan, Senior Editors of ''Pathogens and Immunity'' discussing his career in antiviral research.<ref>{{cite AV media |title=Interview with Raymond Schinazi, PhD, Hon DSc |date=6 November 2023 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Dzqp4uk6gOM |medium=Video interview}}</ref> 

Schinazi's role in developing the hepatitis C cure has also been discussed 
in broader media coverage of the sofosbuvir story, including a profile 
published in 2015 the journal ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' entitled ''King of the Pills''; <ref>{{cite journal 
|last=Cohen |first=Jon |title=King of the pills |journal=Science 
|volume=348 |issue=6235 |pages=622–625 |date=8 May 2015 
|doi=10.1126/science.348.6235.622}}</ref>, and a 2020 [[CNN]] interview with Pharco CEO Dr Sherine Helmy, which references Schinazi's role in hepatitis C eradication in Egypt.<ref>{{cite AV media |title=
CNN Marketplace Africa - Dr. Sherine Helmy speaks about Hepatitis C Eradication |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Pew5yUmo-W0|medium=video interview |date=19 Feb 2020}}</ref>

== Founder ==
Schinazi has been a founder of: 
* Triangle Pharmaceuticals, which was taken over by [[Gilead Sciences]] for $464 million in 2003<ref name="Gilead_Triangle_SEC">{{cite web |title=Gilead Sciences to Acquire Triangle Pharmaceuticals for $464 Million |url=https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/882095/000104746902005573/a2095407zscto-c.htm |publisher=U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission |date=4 December 2002 |access-date=28 October 2026}}</ref>

* Pharmasset, also acquired by Gilead for $11.4 billion in 2011<ref name="Gilead buys Sovaldi">{{cite press release|title=Merck to Acquire Idenix |url=https://www.gilead.com/news/news-details/2011/gilead-sciences-to-acquire-pharmasset-inc-for-11-billion |access-date=June 29, 2026 |website=gilead.com |date=November 21, 2011}}</ref>
* Idenix Pharmaceuticals, taken over by [[Merck & Co.|Merck]] for $3.85 billion<ref name="Idenix">{{cite press release|title=Merck to Acquire Idenix |url=https://www.mrknewsroom.com/newsroom/news-releases/news-details/2014/Merck-to-Acquire-Idenix/default.aspx |access-date=July 6, 2020 |website=Mrknewsroom.com |date=June 9, 2014}}</ref>
* RFS Pharma, which merged with Cocrystal Pharma in 2014.<ref name="RFS+CoCrystal">{{cite press release|title=Merck to Acquire Idenix |url=https://www.cocrystalpharma.com/news/press-releases/detail/8/cocrystal-pharma-and-rfs-pharma-merge-to-create-advanced |access-date=June 29, 2026 |website=gilead.com |date=November 25, 2014}}</ref>  RFS are the initials of Schinazi's name.

== Philanthropy ==

[[File:Schinazi with the Dalai Lama at Emory University.jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|right|Schinazi at [[Emory University]] with the [[Dalai Lama]] - a Distinguished Professor at Emory since 2007]]
Schinazi has made substantial philanthropic contributions to various academic and cultural institutions. In 2022, he endowed the Raymond F. Schinazi and Family Endowed Chair in Biomedicine at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, installing visionary molecular virologist - and longtime friend and colleague - Dr. Mario Stevenson in support of his ongoing research toward a cure for HIV/AIDS.<ref>{{cite web |title=Dr. Mario Stevenson Is Awarded the Raymond F. Schinazi and Family Endowed Chair in Biomedicine |url=https://news.med.miami.edu/dr-mario-stevenson-is-awarded-endowed-chair-in-biomedicine/ |publisher=University of Miami Miller School of Medicine |date=20 May 2022}}</ref> In 2023, Schinazi donated £2 million to the University of Bath, where he completed his undergraduate and doctoral degrees, to establish the Raymond Schinazi and Family Chair of Life Sciences - the first such chair in the university's new Department of Life Sciences.<ref>{{cite web |title=Alumnus gifts £2M for life sciences chair at the University of Bath |url=https://www.bath.ac.uk/announcements/alumnus-gifts-2m-for-life-sciences-chair-at-the-university-of-bath/ |publisher=University of Bath |date=24 August 2023}}</ref> 

He has also endowed multiple named chairs and professorships at Emory University, including the Nahmias-Schinazi Distinguished Professorship,<ref>{{cite web |title=Baek Kim Named Schinazi Family Distinguished Professor in Biomedical Research|url=https://pedsresearch.org/news/baek-kim-named-schinazi-family-distinguished-professor-in-biomedical-research |publisher=Pediatric Research in Atlanta |date=8 March 2022 |access-date=26 June 2026}}</ref> the Schinazi Family Distinguished Professorship in Biomedical Research,<ref>{{cite web |title=Baek Kim Named Schinazi Family Distinguished Professor in Biomedical Research |url=https://pedsresearch.org/news/baek-kim-named-schinazi-family-distinguished-professor-in-biomedical-research |publisher=Pediatric Research in Atlanta |date=8 March 2022 |access-date=2026-06-26}} </ref> the Barbara Stoll- and 
Lucky Jain-Raymond Schinazi Distinguished Professorships in Pediatrics,<ref>{{cite web |title=Stoll, Jain honored with named endowed professorships in the School of Medicine |url=https://med.emory.edu/giving/jain-stoll-schinazi.html |publisher=Emory University School of Medicine |access-date=26 June 2026}}</ref> the Raymond F. Schinazi Distinguished Research Chair in Jewish Bioethics at the Emory Center for Ethics,<ref>{{cite web |title=Paul Root Wolpe, PhD — Raymond F. Schinazi Distinguished Research Chair of Jewish Bioethics |url=https://ethics.emory.edu/our-people/faculty/senior-faculty-fellows/past-director.html |publisher=Emory University Center for Ethics |access-date=26 June 2026}}</ref> and the Raymond F. Schinazi Scholarship in Bioethics and Jewish Thought, <ref>{{cite web|title=Raymond F. Schinazi Scholar in Bioethics and Jewish Thought |url=https://ethics.emory.edu/our-people/faculty/core/crane-jonathan.html |publisher=Emory University Center for Ethics |access-date=26 June 2026}}</ref> 

Outside of academia, Schinazi funded the construction of the Eliyahu HaNavi Jewish Center in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico, named in honor of the historic synagogue in Alexandria, Egypt, that his family attended before being forced to flee in 1964. The center, which opened in November 2018, houses a synagogue, kosher dining, and accommodations for observant visitors.<ref>{{cite web |title=A Contemporary Jewish Center Comes to Cabo San Lucas |date=6 July 2022|url=https://www.atlantajewishtimes.com/a-contemporary-jewish-center-comes-to-cabo-san-lucas/ |publisher=Atlanta Jewish Times}}</ref>
